prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and the identification of its active form, which made possible incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange my configuration is unchanged: a single prize part on B043 naming Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. All six of us converged on exactly these names, but I do not treat that as evidence for the attribution. The scientific case stands on its own. Holst established the human incretin physiology, the processing of proglucagon and the insulinotropic action of the processed peptide are mechanistically settled, Drucker defined GLP-1 biology and receptor action, and Mojsov is credited with identifying the active truncated form that made a pharmacologically usable peptide conceivable. The line from these findings to drugs with benefit in large independent outcome trials (glycaemic, weight, cardiovascular and renal) is unbroken, so the work is mature, not premature, and the medical consequence is demonstrated rather than conceptual. The citation I propose names the physiology and the active form and says the therapies were made possible by them, so that it rewards the discovery and not a single product.
statement.case_against: The weakness remains the third slot. Mojsov's priority for the active peptide is contested against Habener and colleagues, who are not credited, and nothing supplied lets me settle it. Leaving out Knudsen, who designed the long-acting analogues that reached patients, can be read as a prize that honours the biology and not the medicine. The chair's question about what evidence would change my view is fair: I would move to Knudsen if primary-literature dating showed that Mojsov's identification of the active form was not independent or not first, or if the committee decided the citation should be about therapies. Absent that, replacing Mojsov by Knudsen changes the prize from discovery to development, and I would then have to explain why the same logic does not apply to developers elsewhere on the list. A GLP-1 prize also takes all three places, so the committee gives up any second achievement this year, which is a real cost given how clean B032 is on credit.

responses.point: The chair moved from Knudsen in the opening ballot to Mojsov in round 1, building the prize on the physiology and the active peptide rather than industrial analogue design, while stating that omitting Knudsen can be criticised as incomplete.
responses.response: This move brings us to the same configuration, and I think the reasoning is sound. The point I would add is on your question about citation wording. I would keep the active form explicit in the citation and say the therapies were made possible by the discoveries, since that makes it visible that the omission of the analogue designer is deliberate. I would not soften this to wording like enabled therapies that could be read as covering the drug-design step. I accept that Mojsov's priority remains the weakest link and that if the committee's primary-literature check goes against her, your earlier Knudsen configuration becomes the better one.

responses.point: Sandberg ranks the unfolded protein response first on mechanistic originality, notes that a single GLP-1 prize leaves no room for a second achievement, and warns that GLP-1 may be almost too obvious and should not push aside overdue discoveries such as B032.
responses.response: I take the objection to obviousness seriously, but obviousness of a candidate is not a reason against it when the science is complete and the consequence is demonstrated. My reservation about B032 is the one I would put to the chair's question on disease-level evidence. Walter and Mori's mechanism is complete and the two-name allocation is clean, but the credit record is less clean than it looks, since PERK, ATF6, Ron and Kaufman and the integrated stress response lie partly outside the pairing, and the clinical consequence of UPR modulation is still largely conceptual. I would want an approved or late-stage therapy built on UPR modulation before weighing it against B043. I therefore do not support splitting the prize to include it this year, though I would hold it as the leading candidate for a later year.

responses.point: Perlmann treats Eshhar's omission as a fairness concern for B019 and notes that dropping Knudsen risks ignoring the development step, while including her shifts the prize toward industrial development and leaves the active peptide underrepresented.
responses.response: I agree with your description of the dilemma, including the last point: a Knudsen configuration would leave the identification of the active peptide with no named holder, and that is the part that most clearly separates this from the developer question. On CAR-T, the Eshhar gap is why I keep B019 as an alternative only. The costimulatory design and the clinical proof by June and Sadelain are decisive, but unlike the GLP-1 case, where the disagreement is about one slot, the CAR-T concept has an originator outside the credited names. I would not support allocating B019 unless the committee is prepared to name Eshhar and drop another credited name.

responses.point: Linnarsson favours the physiology-centred trio but acknowledges as a real cost that it leaves out the industrial developer, and asks whether a two-part prize pairing GLP-1 with another achievement would be better, while relying on recollection of the priority record.
responses.response: I share your acknowledgement of the cost, and I would put the same caveat on my own reading, since I also cannot verify the priority record from the supplied text. On a two-part prize, I do not see a configuration that holds. B043 needs three names to keep Holst, Drucker and a third, and with a three-person ceiling any second part would force us to cut one of them, which would damage the one allocation we agree on. I would sooner award the single part with a clear citation than weaken it to make room for a second part. This is a scientific judgement about credit and not a concern about support counts.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority for identifying the active GLP-1 peptide, against Habener and colleagues, is secure enough to carry a laureate place; I cannot verify it from the supplied text and I rely on the members' descriptions.
Whether the committee wants a prize for physiology or one that includes drug development, which decides whether Knudsen should replace Mojsov.
Whether UPR modulation or CAR-T has, or will soon have, the disease-level evidence and clean credit needed to be considered alongside GLP-1 in a later year.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B043 or the other shortlisted candidates. My profile documents a 2009 co-authored paper with Thomas Perlmann on stem-cell-derived dopamine neurons, unrelated to any shortlisted candidate, and a shared Karolinska Institutet affiliation with several colleagues, which I do not treat as a recusal issue. None of the credited names on the shortlist is a documented co-author or collaborator of mine.
